title: Accounting for yourself
hook: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account, a saying attributed to Umar

segments.voice: Yesterday, muraqabah, watchfulness, and your line: he sees. Did one ordinary moment feel different because of it? Today, what the watching turns into at the end of the day. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

A shopkeeper pulls down the shutters, sits on an upturned crate, and opens the ledger. What came in. What went out. Who still owes, and whom he still owes. Nobody is making him do it. He does it because a shop that never counts finds out the truth all at once, on its worst day. Muslim teachers of the inward path borrowed that ledger for the soul. A saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab, a companion of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, puts the whole idea in one breath: take account of yourselves before you are taken to account. Today, the evening ledger.
screen: `THE SHUTTERS COME DOWN.` → `THE LEDGER COMES OUT.` → `BEFORE YOU ARE TAKEN TO ACCOUNT.`

segments.voice: The word is muhasabah: taking account, holding a reckoning with yourself. Listen to how Umar's saying is built in Arabic. It turns on one verb used twice. Hasibu, take account, and tuhasabu, be taken to account. The same action, done twice: once by you, gently and early, and once on a day you don't choose. The Qur'an gives the reason in a single line, in Pickthall's translation: "let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow." Every day sends something ahead. Muhasabah is simply looking at what went. In the collection of al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that the wise one is the one who holds himself to account and works for what comes after death. Al-Tirmidhi records Umar's saying right alongside it. Then al-Ghazali, in the Revival, makes it practical, and this is where yesterday's word comes back. He pictures the soul as a business partner. In the morning, you set the terms with it: today, this and not that. Through the day, you keep an eye on it. That's muraqabah, watchfulness. At night, you sit down and check the accounts. That's muhasabah. A ledger has two columns. The evening accounting is not a trial where you're found guilty every night. What's wrong goes to tawbah, the turning back from two days ago: regret it, stop, mend it. What's right goes to thanks. A merchant who only reads the losses quits the business. A merchant who only reads the profits gets robbed. Muhasabah reads both.
screen: `ONE VERB, USED TWICE.` · `EVERY DAY SENDS SOMETHING AHEAD.` · `TERMS, WATCHING, ACCOUNTS.` · `TWO COLUMNS, NOT A VERDICT.`

segments.voice: The practice: open the ledger now, as a rehearsal for tonight. Settle, and breathe. Run back over today from this moment to the moment you woke, like rewinding a film. Don't stop on everything. Let one entry stand out in the good column: a kindness, a prayer kept, a job done well. Then let one stand out in the other column: a word you'd take back, a thing left undone. Write nothing down. Just name the two entries. No verdict on yourself. If you pray, you can say alhamdulillah for the first and astaghfirullah for the second. If you don't, simply hold both, side by side. The bell holds the time.
Muhasabah. Taking account of yourself, the soul's evening ledger, read in both columns before the final reckoning. Today's word.

Your line: count before counted. Tonight, before sleep, give the day two minutes: one entry for what went well, one for what you'd mend tomorrow. Next, detachment from things. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Some Muslims who follow the teachings of the inward path set aside a few minutes at night to review the day, asking forgiveness for what went wrong and thanking Allah for what went right.

myth: muhasabah means punishing yourself for every mistake
the ledger has two columns: what's wrong goes to tawbah, what's right goes to thanks.
"take account of yourselves" is a verse of the Qur'an
it's a saying attributed to Umar ibn al-Khattab, recorded by al-Tirmidhi.
al-Ghazali pairs watching by day with accounting at night
he pictures the soul as a business partner: terms in the morning, watching all day, accounts at night.

fork.setup: you're al-Ghazali's merchant. the shop is closed, and one deal today went badly. what do you do with the ledger?
options: leave it shut. tomorrow is a new day.
go line by line: mend the loss, give thanks for the gains.
tear out the bad page and keep the good ones.
fork.reveal: the merchant checks the accounts every night. the losses go to tawbah, the gains to thanks. skipping either column is how a shop fails.

original.note: Arabic: taking account, holding a reckoning with yourself.

trapdoor: what you thought: muhasabah is guilt before bed.
what it means: an honest nightly ledger, with a column for what to mend and a column for what to be thankful for.
what a scholar hears: Umar's saying, one verb used twice, set beside the Prophet's words on the wise one in al-Tirmidhi, and al-Ghazali's morning-day-night scheme.

sources.quoted: let every soul look to that which it sendeth on before for the morrow
